lesson.title: Nodes, Links, and Messages: How Networks Actually Work
lesson.summary: Covers the basic building blocks of any computer network, nodes, links, packets, and protocols, and shows how a network's shape shapes what happens when part of it fails.
lesson.body:
A network, in the technical sense, is simply a collection of connected points that can exchange information. Each connection point is called a node, and the connections between them are called links. Your home Wi-Fi router is a node. Your laptop is a node. The cable modem that connects your house to your internet provider is a node. A network can be as small as two computers connected by a single cable or as large as billions of devices spread across the planet.

Nodes do not send whole messages across a network as one continuous stream in most modern systems. Instead, information is broken into smaller pieces called packets, each labeled with where it came from and where it is going, similar to how a long letter might be split across several envelopes, each addressed to the same destination and numbered so the recipient can reassemble them in order. Breaking data into packets lets a network share its links efficiently among many senders at once, and lets individual packets take different paths and still arrive to be reassembled correctly.

For nodes to understand each other, they need agreed-upon rules, called protocols. A protocol specifies things like how a message should be formatted, how a node should introduce itself, and what to do if a message does not arrive. This matters because a network is made of many independent devices, often built by different manufacturers and running different software, that nonetheless have to interpret the same signals the same way. Without a shared protocol, a message from one device would be meaningless noise to another, the way a spoken sentence in an unfamiliar language conveys nothing useful even though the sound waves arrive intact.

Networks also differ in shape, or topology. In a star topology, every node connects through one central hub, similar to spokes meeting at the center of a wheel; if the hub fails, connected nodes lose their link to each other. In a mesh topology, nodes connect to several other nodes directly, so a single failure is less likely to cut off the whole network, at the cost of needing more connections to maintain. These structural choices recur constantly in computing, and they matter well beyond plumbing: who a network's central points are, and what happens if those points fail or misbehave, shapes what kinds of trust that network can support.

A related idea worth naming here is bandwidth, the amount of data a link can carry in a given amount of time. Just as a narrow pipe limits how much water can flow through it regardless of how much pressure pushes on the other end, a link with low bandwidth limits how much data can move across it, which is why a network can slow down when many nodes try to send large amounts of information over the same shared link at once.

Understanding nodes, links, packets, and protocols is the foundation for two ideas covered next: how these pieces combine into the specific architecture of the internet, and how different arrangements of those same nodes, centralized versus peer-to-peer, lead to very different answers to the digital trust problem from the previous chapter.
